summary:
Magdalena department stands under Colombia's national legal framework. Legal gender recognition has rested on self-recognition without a surgical requirement since Constitutional Court jurisprudence of 1993, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a declaration before a notary. The earlier route, under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, no longer applies. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011, the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and trans people have been permitted to serve openly in the armed forces since 2015.

That framework operates alongside lethal, organised violence. Colombia recorded 41 trans women killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024; 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. On 5 April 2025 video showed Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was" and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Armed groups circulate named kill lists: in Guajira, flyers posted since March 2024 state that trans people, along with others, "will be military targets", and in Caquetá, "social cleansing" flyers preceded an ultimatum giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed.

Enforcement does not match the statute. An activist quoted in the Guardian investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings of trans women as ordinary cases. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses on presentation of a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers.

Access to public and commercial premises is protected by court order. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (guards at the Cosmocentro mall in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (police at the Santa Marta boardwalk) address entry to such premises for trans people.

No finding on law, enforcement practice, facilities or incidents affecting trans people specific to Magdalena appears in the sourced material; two of the four sources record that absence directly. The national figures above are the baseline against which Magdalena is assessed.
tangentialFactors:
Judgment T-301 of 2004 concerns police at the boardwalk in Santa Marta, the capital of Magdalena, and is cited among the rulings protecting trans people's entry to public premises. It is the only source item with a location inside the department; the sources do not set out the underlying facts, and no later enforcement practice in Santa Marta is sourced.

Colombian society is described as generally conservative on LGBT issues. An Invamer poll of October 2019 recorded 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time, with 47% opposed, a narrow margin that situates formal legal protection in a divided public climate.

The armed-group targeting documented in the sources is regional rather than national in incidence but national in consequence: Caquetá and Guajira are cited as examples of a pattern of conflict-linked lists and "social cleansing" campaigns that continues after the Millerey case. Whether comparable armed-group activity operates in Magdalena is not addressed by any source.

Colombia was the fourth Latin American country to legalise same-sex marriage, a comparison point for regional standing that does not indicate department-level conditions.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
